description:
We were a group of students from St Michael dreaming for the stars. With common roots, even in our university days @ UTP, we share kindred love for the stars.

We are a group of 5. An artist, a 3D modeller, a coder.
summary: Mars Base 7 is a Roblox game where young learners run a small Martian outpost and keep their crew alive for seven Martian Days. Each sol the crew shares only three power cells, but five stations need power, namely Solar Panels, Oxygen Generator, Greenhouse, Shield Bunker and Rocket Fuel Plant. Players walk to each station and decide what to power and what to leave off. At the end of every day a report shows the cause and effect, no power for the Greenhouse means less food for you, no Shield Bunker means more radiation. Random events add pressure. Dust storms block solar power, solar radiation storms send everyone you for the bunker, and micrometeorites puncture air pipes. To win, players must survive and make enough fuel to launch home, balancing short-term survival against long-term goals of escaping. Each day ends with a “Did you know?” fact checked against NASA sources that links to real missions like Opportunity, MOXIE and Curiosity’s radiation detector. The game turns real engineering trade offs into simple playable decisions. Kids learn why mission planners must prioritise life support, power and protection, and that it is smart choices which decides whether a mission succeeds. It works solo or in co-op.
details:
"Stranded on MARS - Balancing Resources & Surviving This Harsh World" is a Roblox game where players run a small Martian outpost for seven martian days. Each day the crew shares only three power cells, but five stations need power

Solar Panels: gives extra power cell next day

Oxygen Generator: Keep crew's air supply active

Greenhouse: grows food so you dont die of starvation

Shield Bunker: protects against radiation

Rocket Fuel Plant: makes fuel to escape

Players walk to each station and press E to plug in a cell, and can unplug to change their minds. At the end of each day, every station raises or lowers a crew meter. A report shows the cause and effect, for example Greenhouse OFF → Food −30 . If Oxygen, Food or Health reaches zero the mission fails. A screen then explains what went wrong, why, and what to try next time. To win, players must survive all seven days and make enough fuel for the rocket launch.

Random events add pressure and fun

Dust storms block sunlight and reduce vision, so the Solar Panels give no bonus cell.

Solar radiation storms sound an alarm. Players have 15 seconds to reach the Shield Bunker, which only opens if itt has power.

Micrometeorites puncture air pipes, and the crew must fix the leak quickly.

Benefits and intended impact

Space content for kids often skips the hard part. Real missions are about trade offs. This game makes those trade-offs the fun. Players learn that:

investing in power pays off later

Life support comes first when resources run low

protection against radiation matters on a planet with no global magnetic field

short term survival has to be balanced against long term goals

Every day ends with a “Did you know?” card for knowledge, checked against NASA sources. The cards connect to real missions. The 2018 dust storm that ended Opportunity’s mission, MOXIE making oxygen on Mars, Curiosity’s radiation measurements, and the Veggie plant system on the Space Station. Our goal is for students to understand why mission planners make the decisions they do.

Tools and technology

Roblox Studio and Luau for the game, with a modular code structure

Rojo to manage the code

Python to analyse the place file

Code generated terrain and user interface. Mars gravity set to about 38% of Earth’s

What makes it creative

Each player is a crew member walking around a living outpost, not clicking through menus.

A tutorial camera tour introduces each station.

Every decision has a visible consequence. Like lights turning on, doors locking, alarms ringing, the rocket launching.

It works solo or in co op, so students must divide jobs like a real crew.

Factors we considered

Age-appropriate design: large text, short sentences, clear cause and effect.

Scientific accuracy: every fact was checked against NASA sources.

Session length: a full mission takes 9 minutes which is short enough for a classroom.
